title: THE RICH MAN WENT TO HELL… BUT THE POOR MAN’S NAME WAS THE ONE HE NEVER FORGOT
paragraphs: THE RICH MAN WENT TO HELL… BUT THE POOR MAN’S NAME WAS THE ONE HE NEVER FORGOT
The terrifying truth behind Jesus’ story of the rich man and Lazarus—and why the greatest tragedy may not be what happened after death, but what the rich man refused to see while he was alive.
There was a man who had everything money could buy.
Beautiful clothes. Expensive food. A comfortable home. The kind of life other people prayed they could someday afford.
And just outside his gate…
There was another man.
Hungry.
Covered in sores.
So weak that even the dogs came and licked his wounds.
Every day, the rich man had an opportunity to see him.
Every day, Lazarus lay close enough to his gate to be noticed.
And every day, life continued.
Until one day…
Both men died.
And suddenly, the man who had everything discovered that everything he owned could not purchase one more breath.
The man who had nothing discovered that his suffering had not made him invisible to God.
But here is what makes this story so disturbing.
Jesus did not tell us that the rich man was a murderer.
He did not tell us that he was a thief.
He did not describe him as an adulterer, a violent criminal, or someone openly mocking God.
He described a man who dressed beautifully, ate extravagantly, and lived comfortably while another human being suffered at his gate.
And perhaps that is why this story should make us more uncomfortable than we expect.
Because it is easy to condemn a monster.
It is much harder to recognize the possibility of spiritual blindness in an ordinary, respectable life.
What if one of the most dangerous things about sin is that we can become comfortable enough to stop noticing it?
What if a person can be surrounded by blessings and still be spiritually bankrupt?
And what if the gate separating the rich man from Lazarus was not merely an entrance to his property…
But a picture of what had happened to his heart?
Jesus told this story in Luke 16:19–31. And to understand its depth, we must listen carefully to what He actually said, what He did not say, and why He told it.
Because this is not simply a story about money.
It is a story about the human heart, the authority of God's Word, the danger of refusing repentance, and the eternal seriousness of our response to divine truth.
And when we finally reach its last sentence, we will discover something extraordinary.
Jesus was pointing toward a truth that His own resurrection would bring into even sharper focus.
But first, we must return to the gate.
Jesus begins:
“There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day.” — Luke 16:19, KJV
The Greek text describes him as wearing porphyra (πορφύρα), purple clothing associated with wealth and distinction, and byssos (βύσσος), fine linen.
These details matter.
Jesus is not merely telling us that this man had money.
He is painting a picture of extraordinary privilege.
Purple garments were associated with status and luxury. Fine linen reflected expensive tastes. His daily feasting suggested abundance as a way of life.
Notice the words “every day.”
This was not a wedding celebration.
Not a birthday banquet.
Not a rare occasion when the family gathered around a special meal.
Luxury was his ordinary existence.
And then Jesus shifts the scene.
“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores.” — Luke 16:20, KJV
Suddenly, the camera moves from the banquet table to the ground outside.
From purple garments to wounded skin.
From abundance to hunger.
From a man surrounded by comfort to a man surrounded by suffering.
And Jesus gives the poor man something He does not give the rich man.
A name.
Lazarus.
In Greek, Lazaros (Λάζαρος), a form of the Hebrew name Elʿazar (אֶלְעָזָר), commonly understood to mean “God has helped.”
Think about that.
His circumstances appeared to contradict his name.
Where was the help?
Where was the relief?
Where was the healing?
He was hungry, covered with sores, and dependent upon the mercy of others.
And yet his very name pointed toward the God who had not forgotten him.
There is something profoundly comforting here for anyone who has ever suffered while watching other people prosper.
For the mother who has cried quietly because the bills are overdue.
For the father who works until his body aches and still wonders whether his efforts are enough.
For the believer battling illness while others seem to move effortlessly through life.
For the person who has prayed for years and still wakes up facing the same painful circumstances.
Your suffering is not proof that God has forgotten your name.
Lazarus was lying outside a gate, but he was not outside God's knowledge.
The world may have overlooked him.
The rich man may have treated him as though he were part of the scenery.
But Jesus knew his name.
And that matters.
Because human beings often measure significance by what someone possesses.
God does not.
Yet we must be careful here.
The name Lazarus does not mean that every person who suffers will automatically be saved, nor does the rich man's wealth mean that every wealthy person is condemned.
Scripture never teaches that poverty purchases heaven or that money, by itself, sends someone to hell.
Abraham himself possessed great wealth (Genesis 13:2). Job was prosperous, and God described him as upright (Job 1:1–3). Joseph of Arimathea was rich and became a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 27:57).
The issue is deeper than financial circumstances.
It is what our lives reveal about our relationship with God.
And Jesus is about to expose that issue with breathtaking force.
Luke 16:21 tells us Lazarus desired to be fed with the crumbs falling from the rich man's table.
Imagine being so hungry that leftovers become a dream.
Not a feast.
Not a seat at the table.
Just enough discarded food to survive.
Then comes one of the most painful details:
“Moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.”

In the ancient setting, dogs could be scavenging animals, and their presence underscores Lazarus's humiliation and vulnerability. The text does not explicitly tell us whether their licking soothed his wounds or worsened his suffering.
What it makes unmistakably clear is his helpless condition.
And all of this was happening at the rich man's gate.
Not across the ocean.
Not in a distant country.
Not in some hidden corner of society where the rich man could reasonably claim ignorance.
At his gate.
The Greek word pylōn (πυλών) refers to a gate or gateway, often a substantial entrance.
The gate should have been a place where compassion crossed from abundance into need.
Instead, it became the boundary between two radically different lives.
And this is where the story begins reaching into our own homes.
Because most of us do not own purple robes.
Most of us do not host extravagant banquets every day.
But we do have gates.
Sometimes our gate is the screen we scroll while someone nearby is silently falling apart.
Sometimes it is the door we close because we do not want another person's problems interrupting our peace.
Sometimes it is the church pew where we sing about God's love while refusing to forgive the person sitting a few rows away.
Sometimes it is our ability to explain Scripture beautifully while remaining unwilling to practice its mercy.
And sometimes the person outside our gate is someone we live with.
A spouse who feels emotionally abandoned.
A child who needs our attention more than another gift.
An aging parent waiting for a phone call.
A friend whose cheerful messages conceal a desperate struggle.
Or a stranger whose suffering we have trained ourselves not to see.
Not every need is ours to solve.
We have limitations. Responsibilities. Families to care for. And wisdom matters in how we help.
But the question remains.
Have we allowed comfort to make compassion inconvenient?
Jesus had already been confronting the spiritual dangers of wealth in Luke 16.
Earlier, He declared that no servant can serve both God and money (Luke 16:13).
Luke then tells us something revealing about His audience.
“The Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him.” — Luke 16:14, KJV
They loved money.
And they ridiculed Jesus.
This context matters enormously.
Jesus was addressing people who could possess religious knowledge while resisting the truth that challenged their hearts.
People who knew the Scriptures.
People who understood religious language.
People who could appear righteous before others.
Yet Jesus told them that God knew their hearts (Luke 16:15).
The rich man and Lazarus must be read against that background.
This is not an attack on everyone who has financial resources.
It is a devastating warning against a heart that can treasure wealth, disregard mercy, and remain unmoved by God's revealed will.
Then the story changes.
Without warning.
Without a final conversation.
Without an opportunity to negotiate.
“And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried.” — Luke 16:22, KJV
Did you notice the contrast?
Lazarus dies, and Jesus speaks of angels carrying him to Abraham's bosom.
The rich man dies, and Jesus mentions his burial.
The man who once possessed every earthly advantage cannot carry those advantages beyond the grave.
The man who seemed abandoned is received into comfort.
The expression “Abraham's bosom” translates the Greek kolpos Abraam (κόλπος Ἀβραάμ), an image of closeness, welcome, and honor in Abraham's presence.
In the biblical world, reclining near someone at a banquet could symbolize intimate fellowship.
The picture is not simply that Lazarus escaped poverty.
It is that he was welcomed.
The man who had longed for crumbs now rests in a place of comfort.
The man who had been left outside a gate is no longer excluded.
The reversal is staggering.
But the story becomes even more unsettling when Jesus describes the rich man's condition.
“And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.” — Luke 16:23, KJV
The Greek word translated “hell” in this verse is Hadēs (ᾅδης), often rendered “Hades,” referring to the realm of the dead.
This is not the same Greek word as Gehenna (γέεννα), which Jesus uses elsewhere in warnings about final judgment.
That distinction matters because we should not flatten every biblical term associated with death and judgment into an identical meaning.
Jesus presents the rich man as conscious, distressed, and separated from the comfort Lazarus experiences.
Christians have differed over how literally to interpret the imagery and how this account relates to the intermediate state before the final resurrection and judgment.
Some understand it as a parable using vivid imagery; others regard it as a description of actual events.
Jesus does not explicitly label it a parable, and the use of Lazarus's name has contributed to that discussion. But naming a character does not, by itself, settle the genre.
Whatever position one takes, the warning Jesus communicates must not be dismissed.
Death is not presented as a convenient opportunity to reverse a lifetime of rejecting God's truth.
The story insists that our response to God matters now.
And then comes a sentence that should make every comfortable heart tremble.
The rich man cries:
“Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.” — Luke 16:24, KJV
Now the man who once feasted daily is begging for a drop of water.
The man who possessed abundance is pleading for relief.
The man whose gate Lazarus could not cross now longs for Lazarus to come to him.
And there is something particularly revealing in his request.
He knows Lazarus's name.
The text does not tell us exactly when or how he learned it, so we should not pretend to know.
But within the story, he recognizes Lazarus.
And still, he asks Abraham to send Lazarus to serve him.
Even in his distress, he speaks as though Lazarus can be dispatched to meet his needs.
It is a chilling detail.
Because suffering does not automatically produce repentance.
Fear does not automatically create love.
And recognizing that judgment is real is not the same thing as surrendering to God.
A person can desperately want relief from consequences without truly grieving the sin that led there.
That distinction should search our hearts.
How often do we ask God to remove the pain while refusing to surrender the pride?
How often do we beg Him to repair our circumstances while resisting His correction?
How often do we want forgiveness without repentance, peace without obedience, and the comfort of Christ without the lordship of Christ?
The rich man's words show distress.
They do not record a confession of sin or a request for a changed heart.
We should not invent motives beyond the passage, but we should notice what is missing.
There is no recorded apology to Lazarus.
No acknowledgment of his neglect.
No plea for reconciliation with the God whose Word he disregarded.
Only a request for relief.
Then Abraham answers.
“Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.” — Luke 16:25, KJV
“Son, remember.”
What a devastating phrase.
The rich man is addressed as a descendant of Abraham, but his ancestry cannot deliver him.
Religious heritage is not the same as living faith.
Being raised in a Christian family is not the same as trusting Christ.
Knowing the language of worship is not the same as loving the Lord.
Having your name on a church membership roll is not the same as having your heart transformed by grace.
Abraham's words emphasize the dramatic reversal of their circumstances.
But we must not turn them into a simplistic formula that says the rich man was condemned merely for enjoying good things or Lazarus was comforted merely for enduring bad things.
That would contradict the wider teaching of Scripture.
Salvation is not earned by poverty, generosity, suffering, or any other human achievement.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
The same Gospel that saves a poor beggar can save a wealthy business owner.
The same grace that reaches someone lying in the street can reach someone sitting in a beautiful home.
But saving faith is not indifferent to the people God calls us to love.
James asks what good it is to speak comforting words to a brother or sister who lacks food and clothing while refusing to help meet their needs (James 2:15–17).
First John asks how God's love can abide in someone who has material resources, sees a fellow believer in need, and closes his heart against that person (1 John 3:17).
And Jesus Himself teaches that love for God and love for neighbor belong together (Matthew 22:37–40).
Our acts of mercy do not purchase salvation.
They can, however, reveal whether our professed faith is living and active.
We are not saved because we love the poor. We learn to love our neighbors because the grace of God is changing us.
And if that grace never challenges our selfishness, we have reason to examine what we mean when we say we believe.
The story continues with another terrible image.
Abraham explains that a great gulf has been fixed between the two conditions, so that no one can cross from one side to the other (Luke 16:26).
The Greek word chasma (χάσμα) describes a chasm or gulf.
The separation is presented as fixed.
There is no bridge the rich man can build.
No payment he can offer.
No earthly influence he can summon.
The wealth that once gave him options has become useless.
And that is one of the most sobering realities in the entire account.
Money can buy medicine, but it cannot guarantee another heartbeat.
Money can purchase a magnificent funeral, but it cannot purchase reconciliation with God.
Money can influence people, but it cannot overturn divine judgment.
And a lifetime of religious appearances cannot replace genuine repentance.
Then something unexpected happens.
The rich man changes his request.
He begins thinking about his family.
“I pray thee therefore, father, that thou wouldest send him to my father's house: For I have five brethren.” — Luke 16:27–28, KJV
Five brothers.
Five people still living.
Five people who may be walking toward the same spiritual disaster.
And now the rich man wants Lazarus to warn them.
There is something deeply human about this moment.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to worry about someone you love who has no interest in God.
A son who has wandered from the faith.
A daughter whose heart has hardened after painful experiences.
A husband who believes Christianity is merely another religious system.
A wife who has been wounded by hypocrisy and no longer wants anything to do with church.
A parent who says there will be time to think about eternity later.
We know what it is to want one more conversation.
One more opportunity.
One more chance to say what matters.
But listen carefully to Abraham's response.
“They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” — Luke 16:29, KJV
This is the center of the story's final warning.
The rich man's brothers already possess the testimony of Scripture.
“Moses and the prophets” refers to the Scriptures that revealed God's character, commandments, promises, and demands for justice and mercy.
They were not left without witness.
They did not need to wait for a spectacular supernatural event before taking God's Word seriously.
They needed to listen to what God had already spoken.
And that is astonishing when we remember what the Law and the Prophets repeatedly taught.
Deuteronomy 15 commanded generosity toward the poor.
Isaiah 58 condemned religious observance that ignored injustice and human suffering.
Amos exposed people who lived in luxury while remaining unconcerned about the ruin around them.
Micah 6:8 called God's people to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him.
The rich man's failure was not that God had never revealed His concern for the vulnerable.
The Scriptures had been speaking all along.
The problem was not the absence of revelation.
It was the refusal to hear.
And that brings us to one of the most piercing questions a Christian can face.
What good is a Bible we admire but refuse to obey?
What good is defending biblical truth in public if we deliberately ignore it in private?
What good is knowing the correct theological answer while allowing bitterness, greed, dishonesty, or cruelty to remain unchallenged in our lives?
We can become so accustomed to hearing Scripture that we mistake familiarity for surrender.
We can memorize verses about forgiveness while nourishing resentment.
We can sing about grace while humiliating people who have fallen.
We can preach generosity while worshiping financial security.
We can defend the sanctity of life while treating struggling human beings as inconveniences.
And we can speak endlessly about heaven while refusing to love the people God has placed directly in front of us.
The rich man's story exposes the danger of hearing without responding.
Then comes his final argument.
“Nay, father Abraham: but if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent.” — Luke 16:30, KJV
He believes a miracle will accomplish what Scripture has not.
Surely, if someone returns from the dead, his brothers will listen.
Surely, if they witness something impossible, they will change.
Surely, if the evidence becomes overwhelming, repentance will follow.
But Abraham answers:
“If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.” — Luke 16:31, KJV
And with that sentence, the story ends.
No comforting explanation.
No account of what happened to the five brothers.
No additional scene showing whether they repented.
Jesus leaves His listeners standing before a decision.
Will they hear God's Word?
Or will they continue demanding something more while refusing the truth already given?
But for those of us reading this passage after the resurrection of Jesus Christ, that final sentence carries an extraordinary resonance.
Because someone did rise from the dead.
Jesus Christ.
The One telling this story would Himself be crucified, buried, and raised on the third day.
His resurrection is not merely a dramatic conclusion to a tragic life.
It is central to the Gospel.
The apostle Paul declares that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And yet the New Testament records that not everyone who encountered the testimony of His resurrection believed.
Matthew 28:11–15 describes an attempt to circulate a false explanation of the empty tomb.

John 12:9–11 also records that after Jesus raised another man named Lazarus—the Lazarus of Bethany, who is distinct from the beggar in Luke 16—some religious leaders sought to kill Lazarus because many people were believing in Jesus on account of him.
These passages do not mean evidence is unimportant.
Christian faith is not a demand to abandon reason.
The resurrection of Jesus is proclaimed in Scripture as a real event with witnesses.
But they do show that unbelief is not always simply a shortage of information.
Sometimes the human heart resists the implications of truth.
Because if Jesus really rose from the dead, then He cannot be safely reduced to a moral teacher whose advice we may accept or reject according to convenience.
His resurrection vindicates His identity and demands that we reckon with His claims.
And those claims reach far beyond how we spend our money.
They reach into every hidden chamber of the human heart.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our hypocrisy.
Our selfishness.
Our love of applause.
Our need to control.
Our unwillingness to forgive.
Our habit of appearing spiritually strong while privately running from God.
The story of the rich man and Lazarus is not permission to look down on wealthy people.
It is an invitation to stop looking away from the truth about ourselves.
And that truth is uncomfortable.
Because even if we have never worn purple garments or owned a luxurious estate, we have all sinned.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
The rich man needed mercy.
Lazarus needed mercy.
You need mercy.
I need mercy.
And no amount of charity, religious activity, public admiration, or personal suffering can make us righteous before a holy God.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a warning.
It becomes the greatest hope humanity has ever been given.
Because Jesus did not come merely to tell sinners that judgment is real.
He came to save sinners.
The One who told the story of the rich man and Lazarus entered a world filled with suffering, greed, injustice, and death.
He touched lepers whom others avoided.
He welcomed people whose reputations had been destroyed.
He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He proclaimed good news to the poor.
And He called people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
Then He went to the cross.
Not because He had sinned.
Not because He had failed.
Not because death had power over His righteousness.
But because, in the mystery and glory of God's redemptive plan, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
This does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
It means He, who knew no sin, bore our sin in His saving work so that those united to Him might be made righteous before God.
He endured the cross.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
The grave did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ is alive.
And because He lives, repentance is not a hopeless attempt to repair ourselves.
It is a turning toward the Savior who can forgive, cleanse, and transform us.
That is the difference between mere religious fear and Gospel faith.
Fear may make us tremble at the thought of judgment.
Grace brings us to the feet of Jesus.
Fear may make us desperate to escape punishment.
The love of Christ teaches us to hate the sin that wounds our relationship with God and harms others.
Fear may make us promise to become better people.
The Gospel announces that our deepest need is not simply improvement.
It is new life.
Jesus said:
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3, KJV
The Greek expression gennēthē anōthen (γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν) carries the sense of being born “again” or “from above.”
This new birth is not something money can buy.
It is not something religious heritage can guarantee.
It is the work of God.
And it changes the way we see everything.
Including the person at our gate.
When Christ begins transforming our hearts, generosity becomes more than a public performance.
Mercy becomes more than a convenient act of kindness.
Forgiveness becomes more than a beautiful word.
We begin to recognize that the people around us are not interruptions to our spiritual lives.
They are people made in God's image.
People who need compassion.
People who need truth.
People who need the Gospel.
And sometimes the most powerful evidence that we have heard God's Word is not another argument we win.
It is the neighbor we finally notice.
The person we finally forgive.
The injustice we refuse to ignore.
The secret sin we finally confess.
The money we stop worshiping.
The pride we surrender.
The apology we have been postponing.
The hungry person we choose to feed.
The broken person we refuse to treat as disposable.
Not to earn God's acceptance.
But because we have received mercy we could never deserve.
There is another beautiful truth we must not miss.
The rich man wanted Lazarus to cross an uncrossable chasm after death.
But the Gospel tells us that while we are still alive, God calls us to reconciliation through Jesus Christ.
Jesus is not presented in Luke 16 as a literal bridge across Abraham's chasm, and we should not force that image into the passage.
Yet the wider New Testament gives us something glorious.
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5, KJV
And Jesus Himself declares:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6, KJV
Our hope is not that we can somehow cross into heaven through our own goodness.
Our hope is that Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Through His death and resurrection, He opens the way of reconciliation with God.
And that invitation is being proclaimed now.
While we still have breath.
While there is still opportunity to repent.
While we can still turn to Him in faith.
That is why this story should not leave us merely frightened.
It should leave us awake.
Awake to eternity.
Awake to the seriousness of sin.
Awake to the danger of false security.
Awake to the suffering of people around us.
And above all, awake to the grace of Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years living like the rich man, not necessarily in luxury, but in spiritual indifference.
You have had access to God's Word.
You have heard the Gospel.
You have known what needed to change.
But there has always been another excuse.
Another distraction.
Another tomorrow.
Or maybe you identify more closely with Lazarus.
You have been overlooked.
Misunderstood.
Abandoned.
You have watched people with more resources live comfortably while you struggle to survive.
You have wondered whether God sees you at all.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Jesus did not tell this story to promise that every suffering believer will become wealthy, healthy, or comfortable in this present life.
He did not promise that every injustice would be corrected before death.
But He revealed that earthly circumstances do not determine eternal worth, and that God is not indifferent to the oppressed or the forgotten.
Your present pain is not the complete story.
And if you belong to Christ, your future is secured not by the absence of suffering but by the faithfulness of your risen Savior.
There is hope beyond what you can currently see.
There is grace for what you cannot repair.
There is forgiveness for what you are ashamed to confess.
And there is a Savior who calls sinners to come to Him.
Perhaps the most important question is not whether you are rich or poor.
Perhaps it is whether you have truly heard the voice of God.
Not merely heard a sermon.
Not merely liked a Christian post.
Not merely commented “Amen.”
Not merely shared a verse.
But heard His Word in a way that brings you to repentance, faith, and obedience.
Because a person can spend a lifetime discussing spiritual truth and still refuse to surrender.
And a person who has lived in scandal, shame, and rebellion can come to Jesus Christ and find mercy.
That is why we speak so often about going from scandal to grace.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin should be celebrated.
Not because consequences always disappear when someone repents.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem people whose stories seemed beyond repair.
The thief on the cross had no lifetime left to build a reputation for religious goodness.
Yet when he turned to Jesus, the Savior promised him paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
The apostle Paul had persecuted the church.
Yet the grace of Christ transformed him into a servant of the Gospel (1 Timothy 1:12–16).
Peter denied Jesus.
Yet the risen Christ restored him and called him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Their sins were real.
Their failures mattered.
But their failures were not greater than the mercy of the risen Lord.
And neither is yours.
If you are willing to turn from sin and trust Jesus Christ, you do not have to keep pretending that your past is clean.
You can bring the truth into His light.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can begin walking in newness of life.
And if your faith is genuine, that new life will increasingly change how you treat the people God has placed around you.
The Gospel is not simply about escaping judgment.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ and becoming a person whose life reflects His grace.
And that transformation matters today.
Before the funeral.
Before the final breath.
Before another opportunity to love passes by.
Before the person at your gate becomes someone you wish you had noticed sooner.
So ask yourself something difficult.
Who is your Lazarus?
Not necessarily someone asking for money.
Perhaps someone asking for your patience.
Someone asking for forgiveness.
Someone waiting for a visit.
Someone who needs to hear the Gospel spoken with humility instead of condemnation.
Someone whose suffering you have quietly decided is none of your concern.
And what is the gate you have been unwilling to open?
Pride?
Fear?
Convenience?
Bitterness?
A love of comfort?
A secret attachment to sin?
Do not answer too quickly.
Bring the question before God.
Let His Word search you.
And if something in this story has exposed an uncomfortable truth, do not bury that conviction beneath another distraction.
Respond while you can.
You can pray sincerely, in your own words, or begin here:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have ignored things You have shown me. I have loved my comfort more than I should, and there are places in my heart that need Your mercy. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, change me, and teach me to follow You. Open my eyes to the people I have overlooked. Give me a heart that loves what You love. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen.”
These words are not a magical formula.
Salvation is not earned by reciting a particular prayer.
The call of the Gospel is to repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
And for those who already belong to Him, the call is to continue growing in grace, truth, love, and obedience.
If this message has brought something to the surface that you have been avoiding, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details publicly. A simple request for prayer is enough.
Someone reading may need to know that genuine transformation is possible.
There may also be someone in your life who needs this message.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you have decided they are the rich man in the story.
But because you love them enough to want them to encounter the truth and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Not as another piece of religious content to collect and forget, but as something to revisit when comfort begins to dull compassion or when suffering tempts you to believe God has abandoned you.
And if you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, I invite you to stay connected.
Because the goal is not simply to build an audience.
It is to help people encounter the Word of God and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture more deeply, strengthen their faith, and develop a more consistent walk with Christ.
And for those who feel led to help sustain and expand this work, there is another way to participate.
For believers who prayerfully set aside part of their resources for Christian ministry, that support may be one expression of their generosity and stewardship.
But I want to be very clear about something because the Gospel itself demands it.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
You do not have to purchase spiritual growth, forgiveness, or belonging.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV

The apostle Paul also teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), while the wider New Testament consistently calls believers to generosity and care for those in need.
Let it be an act of willing partnership, never guilt.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as everyday reminders of Scripture, conversation starters about faith, and additional ways to help sustain the work.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand the Bible more clearly, encouraged you through a difficult season, or reminded you to return to Jesus when your heart was drifting, consider becoming part of the community that helps carry this ministry forward.
Pray for those who are hurting.
Encourage someone who is growing weary.
Support faithful Christian teaching where you are able.
Care for the person at your gate.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
And He alone deserves the glory.
Now, before you leave this story, return with me one last time to the two men.
One lived behind a gate.
The other lay outside it.
One was clothed in purple.
The other was covered in sores.
One feasted.
The other longed for crumbs.
Then death came.
And the earthly distinctions that once seemed so important were stripped of their power.
Jesus did not end His story by telling us to become obsessed with the rich man's torment.
He ended by directing attention back to the Word of God.
“They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.”
Hear them.
Listen.
Respond.
And now, having received the testimony of the apostles concerning the crucified and risen Christ, we have even greater reason to take God's revelation seriously.
Do not wait for a voice from the grave to tell you that eternity matters.
Listen to the Savior who conquered the grave.
Do not wait until suffering reaches your own doorstep before learning compassion.
Look for the people God has already placed near you.
Do not mistake religious familiarity for genuine faith.
Come to Christ.
Do not imagine that wealth makes you secure or that poverty makes you forgotten.
Trust the Lord whose grace reaches sinners in every circumstance.
And do not believe that your past must remain the final definition of your life.
The rich man's story is a warning.
But the resurrection of Jesus is a proclamation of hope.
The door of repentance is open now.
The invitation of the Gospel is being proclaimed now.
The call to love your neighbor is before you now.
And the Savior who died for sinners is alive forevermore.
Remember the gate.
Remember Lazarus.
Remember the Word of God.
Remember the empty tomb.
And remember that the Jesus who warns us about judgment is the very Jesus who gave His life so that sinners who repent and believe might be saved.
The tragedy is not that the rich man failed to recognize Lazarus after death—it is that he had a lifetime to show mercy while Lazarus was still at his gate.
